WHAT YOU ALREADY KNOW   What you already know
Book 2, Chapter 18 built the standard cost card and defined the standard quantity allowed. Chapter 11 of this book produced the flexible-budget variance that is now opened up.
Reason for a standard costing system (C.1.j)
Inventory and cost of goods sold are recorded at standard, so every unit carries the same cost
Variances point to what differed from the plan (Chapter 11)
Each variance has an owner: purchasing, the plant, the sales team
The standard card builds the budget (Chapters 6 to 8) and supports price decisions
Clear, attainable targets for each input (Book 2, Chapter 18)

WORKED EXAMPLE   Worked example: concentrate in June
Price: ($0.92 − $0.90) × 437,000 liters = $8,740 unfavorable. Usage: (437,000 − 432,000) × $0.90 = $4,500 unfavorable. Together $13,240, the figure Chapter 11 reported. Figure F312-06 sets out the calculation.
$260 of the variance is carried in stock

EXAM TRAP   Which quantity?
The price variance always uses an actual quantity, bought or used; the usage variance always uses the standard price. Using the standard quantity for the price variance, or the actual price for the usage variance, double-counts part of the difference.

EXAM TRAP   Read the pair, not the single variance
A favorable price variance beside an unfavorable usage variance usually points to one decision, not two separate results. Judging either one alone gives the wrong conclusion.
